body:
What makes an organism living?

An organism is an individual living system. A large banyan tree, a human being and a microscopic bacterium differ greatly in size and structure, but each carries out essential biological activities. These activities allow organisms to obtain materials, use energy, maintain their internal conditions and respond to their surroundings.

The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life. Some organisms, such as many bacteria, consist of a single cell. Others, including humans and most familiar plants, have many cells that perform specialised functions. In a multicellular organism, different tissues and organs work together to maintain life.

Living cells continuously carry out chemical reactions. The combined chemical activities of an organism are called metabolism. Metabolism includes both the breakdown of substances to release usable energy and the formation of substances needed for growth, maintenance and repair.

The principal life processes

Life processMeaningBasic example
NutritionObtaining and using materials needed for energy, growth and repairGreen plants manufacture carbohydrates; humans eat and digest food.
RespirationReleasing usable energy from food through cellular reactionsCells break down glucose to obtain energy.
TransportMoving essential substances and wastes between parts of an organismBlood transports oxygen; xylem transports water.
ExcretionRemoving metabolic waste substancesKidneys remove urea in urine.
Control and responseDetecting changes and coordinating an appropriate reactionA person withdraws a hand from a hot object.
Growth and reproductionIncreasing and developing the organism; producing new individualsA seed develops into a plant that may later produce seeds.

These processes are connected. For example, a human cell receives nutrients through digestion and transport. It uses these nutrients during respiration to release energy. The blood also carries carbon dioxide and other wastes away from the cell. The lungs and kidneys help remove these wastes from the body.

Distinguishing living and non-living things

A single visible characteristic is not sufficient to identify life. A vehicle moves, but its movement does not arise from cellular metabolism. A cloud may increase in size, but it does not grow through cell division. A plant remains rooted in one place, yet it is living and can respond to light, water and gravity.

Likewise, reproduction is important for the continuity of a species, but an individual organism need not reproduce to be alive. An infertile animal and a seed that remains temporarily dormant are not automatically non-living. Dormant organisms or structures may show very little visible activity while retaining the capacity to resume normal biological functioning under suitable conditions.

Organisms and their surroundings

Life processes require inputs from the environment. Green plants use sunlight, carbon dioxide, water and minerals. Animals obtain food directly or indirectly from plants. All organisms interact with surrounding air, water, soil and other living beings. Consequently, a change in environmental conditions can affect both individual health and the survival of populations.

Cellular respiration is not the same as breathing. Breathing moves air into and out of respiratory organs. Cellular respiration releases usable energy from food inside cells.

Prelims focus

  • The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of living organisms.
  • Metabolism includes the chemical reactions that sustain life.
  • Nutrition supplies materials; respiration releases usable energy.
  • Excretion removes metabolic wastes, while transport moves substances within an organism.
  • Trap: Visible movement or reproduction by every individual is not an essential test of whether something is living.

[NCERT, Science, Class 6, Chapter 9, The Living Organisms—Characteristics and Habitats, section 9.4; NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 6, Life Processes, introductory discussion; NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Chapter 1, Reproduction in Organisms, introductory discussion.]

title: Living Organisms and the Processes That Sustain Life

body:
Autotrophic and heterotrophic nutrition

All organisms require nutrients, but they obtain them in different ways. Autotrophs manufacture organic food from simple inorganic substances using an energy source. Green plants, algae and certain bacteria are autotrophs. Heterotrophs depend on organic substances produced by other organisms. Animals, fungi and many microorganisms are heterotrophs.

Most green plants prepare food through photosynthesis. Chlorophyll-containing cells absorb light energy and use it to convert carbon dioxide and water into carbohydrates. Oxygen is released during the process.

Oxygen-producing photosynthesis is the process through which chlorophyll-containing organisms use light energy to manufacture organic food from carbon dioxide and water, releasing oxygen.

Materials and structures involved

  • Carbon dioxide: Enters leaves mainly through tiny pores called stomata.
  • Water: Is absorbed from the soil by roots and transported through xylem.
  • Sunlight: Supplies the energy required for the process.
  • Chlorophyll: Is the green pigment that absorbs light energy. In plants, it is located within chloroplasts.
  • Carbohydrate: Is produced and may be used immediately, transported to other parts or stored in forms such as starch.
  • Oxygen: Is released as a product of photosynthesis.

The stomata are openings controlled by surrounding guard cells. They permit gas exchange, but water vapour can also escape through them. Plants must therefore balance carbon dioxide uptake with the need to conserve water.

Photosynthesis is not restricted to ordinary leaves

Green stems and other chlorophyll-containing plant parts can also carry out photosynthesis. This is particularly important in many desert plants. In a typical cactus, the green stem performs much of the photosynthesis while spines, which are modified leaves, help reduce water loss.

Some plants obtain nutrients in unusual ways. Cuscuta, commonly called dodder, is a parasitic plant that obtains nourishment from a host plant. Fungi such as bread mould obtain nutrition from organic material by releasing digestive substances and absorbing the resulting simpler nutrients. This is saprotrophic nutrition, not photosynthesis.

Green plants also require mineral nutrients such as nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. They do not obtain all these minerals from carbon dioxide. Roots absorb usable mineral forms from the soil. Certain bacteria help make nitrogen available to plants; for example, nitrogen-fixing bacteria occur in the root nodules of many legumes.

Photosynthesis and respiration are different

FeaturePhotosynthesisCellular respiration
Main functionStores captured energy in organic substancesReleases usable energy from organic substances
Location in green plant cellsChloroplastsPrincipally mitochondria in aerobic respiration
Light requirementRequires lightDoes not directly require light
Typical gases in oxygen-producing photosynthesis and aerobic respirationUses carbon dioxide and releases oxygenUses oxygen and releases carbon dioxide

Plants respire during both day and night because their living cells continuously need energy. Photosynthesis normally takes place when suitable light is available. Consequently, a green plant can carry out photosynthesis and respiration at the same time during daylight.

It is incorrect to state that plants only take in carbon dioxide or that they do not need oxygen. Both photosynthesis and cellular respiration must be considered when discussing gas exchange in green plants.

Why photosynthesis matters to ecosystems

Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy stored in food. Herbivores obtain this food by eating plants, and carnivores obtain it indirectly by eating other animals. Thus, photosynthetic organisms support most familiar food chains. They also play an important role in maintaining atmospheric oxygen.

Prelims focus

  • Autotrophs produce organic food from inorganic materials; heterotrophs depend on organic food sources.
  • In green plants, photosynthesis requires carbon dioxide, water, light and chlorophyll.
  • Stomata facilitate gas exchange; guard cells regulate their opening.
  • Xylem transports water and mineral nutrients in plants.
  • Cuscuta is parasitic; fungi commonly show saprotrophic nutrition.
  • Trap: Green plants respire during both day and night.

[NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 1, Nutrition in Plants, sections 1.1–1.5; NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 6, Life Processes, section on autotrophic nutrition.]

title: Nutrition in Plants and the Importance of Photosynthesis

body:
Why animals digest food

Animals obtain organic food from other organisms, but many food components are too large or complex to be absorbed directly. Digestion breaks complex food substances into simpler, absorbable substances. The resulting nutrients can then reach cells for growth, repair and energy production.

Human nutrition involves several distinct activities. Ingestion is taking food into the body. Digestion is its breakdown. Absorption is the movement of digested nutrients into the blood or lymph. Assimilation is the use of absorbed nutrients by cells. Egestion is the removal of undigested material through the anus.

The main parts of the human digestive system

  1. Mouth: Teeth break food into smaller pieces. Saliva moistens food, and salivary amylase begins the digestion of starch.
  2. Oesophagus: Muscular contractions move swallowed food towards the stomach.
  3. Stomach: The muscular wall mixes food. Gastric acid provides an acidic environment, and pepsin begins the digestion of proteins.
  4. Small intestine: Most chemical digestion and nutrient absorption occur here. Bile produced by the liver helps emulsify fats, while enzymes from the pancreas and intestinal wall help digest food.
  5. Large intestine: Water and salts are absorbed from the remaining material, which is eventually expelled through the rectum and anus.

The inner surface of the small intestine has numerous finger-like projections called villi. They increase the area available for absorption. Digested nutrients enter the circulation and can be delivered to other body parts.

Digestion and absorption are not identical. Digestion produces simpler substances; absorption transfers those substances across the intestinal lining. Egestion removes undigested food, whereas excretion removes metabolic wastes.

Breathing supplies gases; respiration releases energy

Most human cells use aerobic respiration, in which glucose is broken down using oxygen. The process releases usable energy and produces carbon dioxide and water. Much of the released energy is captured in ATP, a molecule cells use to power their activities.

The overall relationship can be expressed in words: glucose and oxygen are used to produce carbon dioxide, water and usable energy.

Breathing, by contrast, is the physical movement of air. During inhalation, the diaphragm contracts and moves downwards while the chest cavity expands. The resulting fall in pressure draws air into the lungs. During quiet exhalation, the diaphragm relaxes and the chest cavity becomes smaller, helping air move out.

The lungs contain numerous small air sacs called alveoli. Oxygen passes from air in the alveoli into nearby blood capillaries, while carbon dioxide passes from blood into the alveolar air. Blood then transports oxygen to tissues, where cells use it during respiration.

How different organisms exchange gases

OrganismMain gas-exchange structureEssential distinction
HumansLungs and alveoliOxygen enters blood from inhaled air.
Most fishGillsOxygen is obtained from water.
InsectsSpiracles and tracheal tubesAir reaches tissues through a branching tube system.
EarthwormsMoist skinGases diffuse across the body surface.
Adult frogsLungs and moist skinBoth structures can participate in gas exchange.
Whales and dolphinsLungsThese aquatic mammals must surface to breathe air.

When oxygen availability is limited

Some cells and microorganisms can obtain energy without oxygen through anaerobic processes. Yeast can convert sugars into alcohol and carbon dioxide during fermentation. In vigorously exercising human muscles, insufficient oxygen supply relative to demand can increase the formation of lactate during energy production.

These processes yield less ATP per glucose molecule than complete aerobic breakdown. Anaerobic activity is not the normal replacement for oxygen-dependent respiration throughout the human body.

Prelims focus

  • The small intestine is the principal site of nutrient absorption in humans.
  • Villi increase the absorptive surface area of the small intestine.
  • The liver produces bile; the pancreas contributes digestive enzymes.
  • Gas exchange in human lungs occurs across the alveoli and surrounding capillaries.
  • Fish generally use gills; insects use spiracles and tracheae; whales use lungs.
  • Trap: Breathing is physical ventilation, not the cellular reaction that releases energy from glucose.

[NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 2, Nutrition in Animals, section 2.2; NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 10, Respiration in Organisms, sections 10.1–10.7; NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 6, Life Processes, sections on nutrition and respiration; NCERT, Biology, Class 11, Chapter 17, Breathing and Exchange of Gases.]
